claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are governed by their differing responses to thermomechanical processing.
The relevant thermomechanical responses are the degree of grain refinement and formation of secondary nanoscale precipitates.
Processing-induced microstructural changes alter strength and ductility through dislocation-grain-boundary interactions.
The equiatomic quinary alloy and its quaternary and ternary derivatives can all be prepared in an as-cast or homogenized single-phase FCC initial state.
Rolling followed by recrystallization annealing can control or induce grain refinement in these alloys.
All investigated alloys must initially have single-phase FCC microstructures.
A finer grain-size distribution produces increased grain-boundary density.
Thermomechanical processing may produce nanoscale incoherent precipitates in some of the candidate alloys.
Grain refinement increases strength through Hall-Petch grain-boundary strengthening.
Compositional differences among the candidate alloys cause differential secondary-phase or precipitate formation.
The combined effects of grain refinement and precipitation can increase strength but may reduce ductility in some subsets.
Relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, subsets attaining finer grains with minimal precipitation will have increased yield strength while maintaining ductility.
Relative to the quinary baseline, subsets forming more precipitates will have comparable or slightly higher strength but lower ductility.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase FCC alloys processed within controlled thermomechanical-processing parameters.
The hypothesis may not apply when processing produces multiphase microstructures or falls outside the specified deformation and annealing parameters.
Grain-growth behavior and kinetics can differ among Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived compositions and are not yet fully understood.
Precipitate-formation kinetics are sensitive to small compositional changes among the subsets.
A lack of correlation between mechanical properties and measured grain refinement or precipitation after identical processing would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention calls for controlled recrystallization annealing, while the conditions state that annealing temperatures are at room temperature. Room-temperature annealing is generally incompatible with inducing recrystallization unless an exceptional low-temperature process is specified.

Precipitate formation is presented as a central mediator and source of predicted property differences, but the boundary excludes alloys that develop multiphase microstructures. Secondary precipitates constitute an additional phase, so the permitted amount and meaning of 'single-phase' are internally unclear.
